title: Standard refund window
body: Refunds are typically honored within 30 days of purchase for unused or unopened items -- adjust this window to match your actual return policy before relying on it.

title: Refunds above a threshold need a second approver
body: Refund requests above a certain dollar amount typically require sign-off from a manager or team lead before processing -- edit this to set the actual threshold and approver your team uses.

title: Escalate abusive or threatening customer contacts
body: A support agent who receives abusive, threatening, or clearly bad-faith contact from a customer should typically escalate to a manager rather than continuing the conversation solo -- edit this to name your actual escalation path and who's on call for it.

title: Chargebacks get flagged, not auto-refunded
body: A chargeback or payment dispute typically shouldn't be auto-refunded on top of the dispute -- it's usually routed to whoever owns billing disputes for manual review first. Verify this matches your actual chargeback process and who owns it.

title: Repeat refund requests from the same customer get flagged
body: A customer requesting more than a small number of refunds in a short window (e.g. 3 in 90 days) is typically worth flagging for manual review rather than auto-approving every request -- adjust the exact count and window to match your own fraud tolerance.

title: Standard self-serve discount ceiling
body: Sales reps can typically offer up to a fixed percentage discount (commonly in the 10-15% range) without further approval -- edit this to your actual self-serve ceiling.

title: Discounts above the ceiling need manager approval
body: A discount above the self-serve ceiling typically needs written manager or deal-desk approval before it's quoted to the customer -- adjust this to name your actual approver and the exact threshold.

title: Multi-year and custom contract pricing goes through deal desk
body: Non-standard pricing -- multi-year terms, custom bundles, non-list SKUs -- typically routes through a deal desk or finance review rather than being quoted directly by a rep. Verify this matches how your org actually reviews custom deals.

title: Discounts are logged, not verbal
body: Any discount offered to a customer should typically be recorded in the CRM or deal record with who approved it, not agreed to verbally and left untracked -- adjust this to your actual system of record.

title: Free extensions and trial credits have a cap
body: Reps can typically extend a trial or issue account credit up to a small cap without approval, with anything larger needing sign-off -- edit the cap and approver to match your actual policy.

title: Pull requests need at least one review before merge
body: Code typically shouldn't merge to the main branch without at least one approving review from someone other than the author -- adjust this if your team uses a different review bar (e.g. two reviewers for production-critical paths).

title: Secrets never go in source control
body: API keys, tokens, and credentials typically should never be committed to the repo, even temporarily -- they belong in a secrets manager or environment variables. Verify this matches your actual secrets-handling setup and rotate anything that leaks.

title: Breaking API changes need a deprecation window
body: A breaking change to a public or internal API typically needs a documented deprecation period and a heads-up to downstream consumers before it ships, rather than shipping as a silent breaking change -- edit this to your actual deprecation window and notification process.

title: Feature flags gate risky changes
body: A change with meaningful blast radius (a new payment flow, a schema migration, a rewrite of a hot path) typically ships behind a feature flag rather than going straight to 100% of traffic -- adjust this to match how your team actually rolls out risky changes.

title: Postmortems are blameless and written down
body: An incident above a certain severity typically gets a written postmortem focused on process and system gaps, not individual blame -- edit this to your actual severity threshold and where postmortems get filed.

title: Sev1 incidents page the on-call engineer immediately
body: An incident that's actively taking down a core product surface for customers typically pages the on-call engineer right away rather than waiting for someone to notice -- adjust the severity definition and paging tool to match your actual setup.

title: Incident commander role is assigned, not assumed
body: Once an incident is declared, someone typically takes the explicit incident-commander role to coordinate response, rather than everyone independently investigating -- edit this to your actual on-call rotation and how that role gets assigned.

title: Status page updates happen on a cadence during an active incident
body: During an active customer-facing incident, status updates typically go out on a regular cadence (e.g. every 30 minutes) even if there's nothing new to report, rather than going quiet -- adjust the cadence and channel to match your own comms process.

title: Rollback is the default first response to a bad deploy
body: If a fresh deploy is the likely cause of an incident, the typical first move is rolling it back rather than trying to fix forward under pressure -- verify this matches your actual rollback tooling and whether it's always the right call for your stack.

title: On-call handoffs include open issues
body: An on-call rotation handoff typically includes a summary of anything still open or worth watching, not a silent handoff -- edit this to your actual handoff process and cadence.

title: Customer-facing data incidents get a compliance heads-up early
body: An incident that may have exposed customer data typically gets flagged to legal or compliance early, even before root cause is confirmed, rather than waiting until the postmortem -- adjust this to name who actually owns that escalation at your org.

title: Production access requires explicit approval, not default org membership
body: Access to production systems and data typically shouldn't be granted by default to every engineer -- it's usually requested and approved per person for a stated reason. Edit this to your actual access-request process and who approves it.

title: Offboarding revokes access same-day
body: When someone leaves the company or changes roles, their access to internal systems, repos, and production typically gets revoked the same day, not on a delayed cleanup pass -- verify this matches your actual offboarding checklist and who owns it.

title: Shared and service credentials get rotated on a schedule
body: Shared logins and service account credentials typically get rotated on a fixed schedule (e.g. quarterly) rather than living unchanged indefinitely -- adjust the cadence and owner to your actual rotation policy.

title: MFA is required for anything touching customer data
body: Any account with access to customer data or production systems typically requires multi-factor authentication, not just a password -- edit this if your actual MFA requirements differ by system or role.

title: Third-party tools get a security review before company data flows into them
body: A new SaaS tool or vendor that will touch company or customer data typically goes through a lightweight security review before it's adopted, rather than being connected ad hoc -- adjust this to your actual review process and who signs off.

title: Access grants are reviewed periodically, not just at request time
body: Standing access to sensitive systems typically gets reviewed on a recurring basis (e.g. quarterly) to catch access nobody remembers granting -- edit the cadence and reviewer to match your actual process.

title: Purchases above a threshold need manager approval
body: A vendor purchase or subscription above a set dollar amount typically needs manager or finance approval before it's signed, rather than being expensed after the fact -- edit the threshold and approver to your actual policy.

title: New vendors handling company data go through a security check
body: A new vendor that will process company or customer data typically gets a basic security and data-handling review before the contract is signed -- adjust this to your actual vendor review process.

title: Auto-renewing contracts get reviewed before the renewal date
body: A vendor contract with auto-renewal typically gets reviewed for continued need and pricing before it renews, rather than renewing silently -- edit this to your actual review cadence and who owns vendor contracts.

title: Single-vendor dependencies above a certain spend get a documented rationale
body: A vendor that a critical process depends on with no backup option typically gets a documented rationale for why, especially above a certain spend level -- adjust this to your actual risk tolerance and threshold.

title: Procurement requests go through one intake channel
body: Vendor and purchase requests typically go through a single intake channel (a form, a Slack channel, a ticket queue) rather than ad hoc asks to whoever has a company card -- edit this to name your actual intake process.

title: Customer data is deleted on a defined retention schedule
body: Customer data typically shouldn't be kept indefinitely by default -- there's usually a retention window after which it's deleted or anonymized. Edit this to your actual retention period per data type, which will vary by what you store and what regulations apply to you.

title: Data deletion requests are honored within a defined window
body: A customer's request to delete their data typically gets honored within a defined window (commonly 30 days) across every system that holds it, not just the primary database -- adjust the window and the systems list to your actual footprint.

title: Production data doesn't flow into non-production environments unmasked
body: Real customer data typically shouldn't be copied into staging, dev, or test environments without masking or anonymization first -- verify this matches your actual data-handling practice and fix any place it doesn't.

title: Sensitive data categories are documented, not assumed
body: What counts as sensitive data at your company (PII, payment info, health data, etc.) typically needs to be written down somewhere everyone can reference, rather than left to individual judgment -- edit this to point at your actual data classification doc, or write one if it doesn't exist yet.

title: Bulk data exports require a stated business reason
body: Bulk exports of customer or user data typically require a stated reason and, above a certain size, an approval -- adjust the threshold and approval step to match your own policy.

title: Offers above a level need a second sign-off
body: A job offer above a certain level or comp band typically needs sign-off from someone beyond the hiring manager (a skip-level, finance, or the founder) before it goes out -- edit this to your actual approval chain and comp bands.

title: References get checked before an offer, not after
body: Reference checks typically happen before an offer is extended, not as a formality afterward -- verify this matches your actual hiring process and adjust it if you handle some roles differently.

title: New hires get access provisioned on day one, not before
body: A new hire's system access typically gets provisioned on their actual start date, not days in advance -- edit this to your actual onboarding checklist and who owns provisioning.

title: Interview feedback is written down before the debrief
body: Interviewers typically submit written feedback before the hiring debrief happens, so the discussion isn't driven by whoever remembers loudest -- adjust this to your actual interview process and tooling.

title: Contractor and full-time hiring follow different approval paths
body: Bringing on a contractor typically has a lighter approval bar than a full-time hire, but usually still needs some sign-off above the requesting manager -- edit this to your actual policy for each hiring type.

title: Expenses above a threshold need manager approval before reimbursement
body: An expense above a set dollar amount typically needs manager approval before it's reimbursed, with smaller expenses auto-approved -- edit the threshold to match your actual policy.

title: Recurring subscriptions get logged somewhere central
body: A new recurring subscription or software purchase typically gets logged in a central place (a spreadsheet, a SaaS management tool) so nobody's tracking spend from memory -- adjust this to name your actual system of record.

title: Travel and client expenses need a receipt above a small amount
body: Expenses above a small dollar amount typically need a receipt attached to the reimbursement request, with smaller ones exempt -- edit the threshold to your actual policy.

title: Company cards have a default spend limit
body: A company card typically comes with a default monthly spend limit that requires a request to raise it, rather than an unlimited default -- adjust the default limit and approver to match your actual policy.
